prompt: A request crosses four services. Every caller retries its downstream operation, and the database keeps failing. Why can a small original request rate become a retry storm?

options.text: Each retry layer adds only one fixed extra database call
options.explanation: A retry above another retry loop can rerun that entire lower loop.

options.text: Only the outermost loop can issue retries
options.explanation: Independent retry loops can all execute unless policy coordinates them.

options.text: Upper-layer attempts rerun lower retry loops, multiplying calls at the failing dependency
options.explanation: Correct. Nested loops amplify the same logical request; choose one retry layer and bound extra traffic.

options.text: The database generates the extra requests by sending errors
options.explanation: The callers generate retries in response to errors; the database does not originate those attempts.

workedExample: Trace one upper-layer retry: it invokes the next service again, which repeats its own attempts. Further layers repeat the pattern. Centralise retry responsibility at the appropriate layer and use an aggregate budget; jitter alone changes timing.

link.title: Timeouts, retries and backoff with jitter (AWS Builders' Library)

prompt: Only the service directly above a dependency retries, with at most three total attempts. As more first attempts fail, what happens without an aggregate retry budget?

options.text: Dependency traffic stays equal to the original request rate
options.explanation: One retry layer still adds its own retries.

options.text: Every original request always makes exactly two attempts
options.explanation: Successful first attempts stop; failed retries may make a third attempt.

options.text: Retry traffic grows, potentially worsening the failure that caused it
options.explanation: Correct. A per-request cap bounds one operation but can still add substantial aggregate work during broad failure.

options.text: Retrying at one layer guarantees the dependency recovers
options.explanation: It avoids nested multiplication but does not create capacity or fix persistent faults.

workedExample: Some first attempts fail and retry; some of those retries fail again. As failures spread, more operations use their full allowance. An aggregate budget limits extra work across operations, while backoff and jitter spread its timing.

link.title: Timeouts, retries and backoff with jitter (AWS Builders' Library)

prompt: A request path is edge → API → orders → inventory → database, and every hop makes up to 3 total attempts, and all attempts fail despite changes to timing. During a database overload, the database sees a retry storm. Which changes reduce the **amplification**? Select all that apply.

options.text: Raise every layer's per-try timeout to 30 seconds
options.explanation: Longer timeouts don't reduce the number of attempts once they fail; they make each layer hold threads and connections longer, spreading the overload upwards.

options.text: Retry only in the layer directly above the database; every other layer fails fast
options.explanation: Correct. One retry layer prevents outer retries from rerunning entire inner retry loops.

options.text: Add a per-client retry budget so retries stay below 10% of requests
options.explanation: Correct. An aggregate budget limits extra retry traffic across requests; define its accounting window and denominator explicitly.

options.text: Have the database return an "overloaded; don't retry" error that upper layers pass up without retrying
options.explanation: Correct. An explicit signal stops every layer above from treating the rejection as a transient fault to retry.

options.text: Add full jitter to every layer's backoff
options.explanation: Jitter does not reduce the worst-case attempt cap when all attempts still fail. In real contention, smoothing load may improve success and thereby reduce actual attempts.

workedExample: Separate how much extra work is permitted from when it arrives. Retry placement, aggregate budgets and explicit do-not-retry signals reduce the maximum offered work. Jitter and timeouts change timing; smoothing can improve real success, but this scenario holds all attempts failing.
